Introduction High-strength ceramic materials have become indispensable in dental and biomedical applications. Within the dental field, in particular for the applications of crowns, fixed dental prosthesis (FDP) and implants, zirconium dioxide (ZrO2) which has garnered significant attention for its superior biocompatibility and exceptional mechanical and optical properties compared to other tooth-colored restorative materials. As a polymorphic material, zirconia exhibits three crystalline phases, namely monoclinic, tetragonal and cubic which transform under specific temperature or stress conditions. Without chemical stabilization, zirconia crystallizes into its cubic phase (c) above 2370°C–2900 °C, transforms into the tetragonal phase (t) at 1770 °C–2370 °C, and into monoclinic phase (m) below 1770 °C. The tetragonal-to-monoclinic (t→m) transformation is accompanied by a volumetric expansion of approximately 3–7 %, which generates internal tension that induces microcrack formation, compromising structural integrity (Guazzato M et al., 2004; Denry and Kelly, 2008, Song et al., 2013; Platt P et al., 2014). The evolution of zirconia ceramics has focused on balancing mechanical durability with optical performance. In order to mitigate these phase transformation challenges, 3 mol% yttria-stabilized tetragonal zirconia polycrystal (3Y-TZP) was developed. Yttria (Y2O3) stabilizes the tetragonal phase at room temperature in a metastable state, enabling the phenomenon of transformation toughening. First-generation 3Y-TZP was widely employed as a framework material veneered with feldspathic ceramics but its high opacity and clinical reports of susceptibility to chipping and fracture limited its broader applications (Pjetursson et al., 2018). Advances in second- and third-generation zirconia have prioritized esthetics by reducing the alumina content and increasing yttria concentration (4–5 mol%) in order to enhance translucency (Nakamura et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016). These modifications, however, come at the cost of reduced mechanical strength and diminished transformation toughening, and heightened susceptibility to low-temperature degradation (LTD) (Stawarczyk et al., 2017). Under mechanical stress, localized t→m transformation induces compressive forces at crack tips, effectively arresting and preventing their propagation. This mechanism is fundamental to the high strength and fracture resistance of conventional zirconia. According to Ritchie (2011), the resistance to crack propagation in ceramics is not solely attributed to microcrack formation or transformation toughening but also a complex interplay of mechanisms that include crack deflection, crack bridging, and crack tip shielding. These extrinsic toughening mechanisms operate primarily in the crack wake region, acting to reduce the local driving force for crack growth. In zirconia, transformation toughening is particularly effective because the stress-induced transformation from the metastable tetragonal to monoclinic phase produces a volumetric expansion and shear strain near the crack tip, generating compressive stresses that counteract crack opening. Thus, while t→m phase transformation contributes to toughness, it is part of a broader framework of fracture resistance strategies described in ceramic materials (Ritchie, 2011 ). In the oral cavity, zirconia restorations are exposed to saliva, fluctuating temperatures, acidic conditions, and cyclic masticatory forces where a gradual conversion from the tetragonal to the monoclinic phase is triggered by water diffusion into the crystal lattice at temperatures between ∼30 °C and 400 °C leading to a phase transformation phenomenon known as low temperature degradation (LTD) (Kobayashi et al., 1981; Chevalier et al., 2009a, Chevalier et al., 2009b; Borchers et al., 2010; Koenig et al., 2016). This significant increase in the monoclinic phase over time results in surface roughening, microcrack formation, and a progressive decline in mechanical properties, as observed in fatigue studies, threatening the long-term success of restorations (Deville et al., 2004b; Kelly and Denry, 2008; Chevalier et al., 2009a; Yang et al., 2021). Standards such as ISO 13356:2008 require limiting monoclinic phase transformation to less than 25 % to ensure biomedical reliability of zirconia (International Standards Organization, 2015, Lughi and Sergo, 2010). In addition to the polishing process that is commonly performed in the dental lab, clinical adjustments to zirconia-based restorations are frequently required to optimize fit, contour, and occlusal or proximal contact (Hmaidouch et al., 2014). These adjustments typically involve grinding with diamond burs of medium or coarse grit size (Pereira et al., 2016). Grinding can significantly alter surface characteristics of zirconia increasing roughness, modifying topography and introducing surface defects (Guilardi et al., 2017) that might act as stress concentration zones, increasing the risk of mechanical failure. Controversially, it has also been pointed out that grinding can generate compressive stresses on the surface, which in turn could increase flexural strength but excessive or uncontrolled transformation may have a trade-off in terms of reduced reliability (Kosmac et al., 2000 ). The extent of phase transformation is influenced by factors such as grain size, material composition, and surface treatment methods. Grinding with coarse diamond burs, for example, has been shown to significantly increase monoclinic content, as confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses (Ramos et al., 2016). fetched_contents.text: Estimation of the phase diagram for the ZrO2–Y2O3–CeO2 system Abstract Comprehensive descriptions of the thermodynamic properties and experimental information in three oxide systems ZrO2–Y2O3, ZrO2–CeO2 and Y2O3–CeO2 are given and thermodynamic models for the calculation of these systems are discussed. The phase diagrams of the quasi-ternary ZrO2–Y2O3–CeO2 system in the zirconia-rich corner are estimated at different temperatures with a substitutional model and Muggianu's extrapolation. The equilibrium phase diagram calculation is extended to low temperatures, as well as the Gibbs free energy of the tetragonal, monoclinic and cubic phases of zirconia doped with yttria and ceria. Introduction ZrO2-containing ceramics are of great importance in many applications such as high temperature electrolytes in fuel cells, magnetohydrodynamic electrodes, oxygen gas sensors, heat-resistant linings of high temperature furnaces, biomaterials, and others.1, 2 Besides, due to the stress induced martensite transformation occurring in this material, through which the metastable tetragonal phase can spontaneously transform to the monoclinic phase, an associated shape memory effect might yield another tremendous potential for applications of this material. Moreover, ZrO2-containing ceramics also find their way to applications in the engineering field. Since YSZ is usually used with electrodes at high temperatures, it is necessary for YSZ to have almost the same thermal expansion coefficient as them over the whole temperature range used. Therefore, the study of the thermal expansion is important to design a system composed of such composite materials. Not only for such a practical purpose, but also from a theoretical point of view, the study on the thermal expansion is important, because it is one of the most important thermodynamic properties. Undoped zirconia has a monoclinic structure and doping about 2 mol% Y2O3 stabilizes to be a mixing of cubic and tetragonal structure [5]. Tsukuma et al. Mini-report on the phase-stability effects of yttria doping in zirconia

Yttria doping stabilizes zirconia by suppressing the monoclinic phase and stabilizing the tetragonal or cubic phase at room temperature. The stabilization mechanism operates through substitutional solid-solution formation, where Y³⁺ cations replace Zr⁴⁺ sites in the crystal lattice, and the yttrium ions bond with oxygen atoms within the zirconia lattice, helping to maintain structural stability [N1-R1][N1-R5]. In this sense, yttria doping is not simply a compositional change but a solid-solution-mediated stabilization strategy.

The phases affected by yttria doping are well established. Pure ZrO₂ is monoclinic at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, and it undergoes phase transformation from monoclinic to tetragonal at about 1170 °C and then to cubic at about 2370 °C [N3-R1]. Yttria doping suppresses the spontaneous monoclinic phase at low temperatures and stabilizes the tetragonal/cubic structure in a metastable state. The evidence base here is direct: the stabilization mechanism is described as making the cubic crystal structure stable at room temperature in yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) [N1-R3], and the same source states that yttria doping stabilizes the tetragonal phase [N1-R4]. The broader thermodynamic picture is also consistent: yttria doping is linked to the formation of stabilized Zr(Y)O₂ and can suppress perovskite formation in some compositions, although the exact relationship depends on the doping level and phase [N4-R5].

The role of solid-solution formation is central. The mechanism is explicitly substitutional solid solution formation, where Y³⁺ replaces Zr⁴⁺ and the solid solution is a key pathway to stabilization [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Cation ordering also appears relevant. In the ZrO₂–Y₂O₃ system, long-range ordering occurs at 40 mol% Y₂O₃, and an ordered phase Zr₃Y₄O₁₂ is reported with rhombohedral symmetry and a decomposition temperature above 1250±50 °C [N4-F2]. This shows that yttria doping does not merely broaden the solid solution; it can induce ordering, which itself modifies phase stability.

The dependence on temperature is clear. Pure ZrO₂ is monoclinic at room temperature and becomes tetragonal above about 1170 °C, then cubic above about 2370 °C [N3-R1]. Yttria stabilization shifts the stability field so that the cubic or tetragonal phase can remain metastable at room temperature [N1-R3]. The stabilization is therefore strongly temperature-dependent, because the same yttria content can alter which phase is stable at different thermal regimes. The evidence also suggests that stabilization is not universal across all yttria levels: the phase diagram and thermodynamic models indicate a broad compositional range of stabilization but also limits and exceptions [N4-F1][N4-F2]. Pressure dependence is not directly discussed in the provided evidence, so any claim about pressure effects must be treated as unsupported in this set of sources [N7].

Overall, yttria doping stabilizes tetragonal or cubic zirconia at room temperature, suppresses the monoclinic phase in some conditions, and is mediated by solid-solution formation and cation ordering. The stabilization range is therefore composition-dependent, and the exact phase behavior shifts with yttria content and temperature [N1-R1][N1-R3][N3-R1][N4-F2].
node_outputs.N8:
Mini-report on phase-transition temperature changes caused by yttria doping

Yttria doping generally raises the temperatures at which monoclinic–tetragonal and monoclinic–cubic transitions occur. The basic behavior of pure zirconia is that monoclinic is stable at room temperature, then transforms to tetragonal at about 1170 °C and then to cubic at about 2370 °C [N3-R1]. Yttria-stabilized zirconia, by contrast, is described as having the cubic crystal structure stable at room temperature, and the retained tetragonal phase is the defining feature of YSZ in some contexts [N1-R3][N1-R4]. This indicates that yttria doping shifts the phase boundaries upward: the transition temperatures increase, and the metastable tetragonal phase can be retained at lower temperatures.

The evidence also suggests that the transitions can become sharper or more diffuse depending on yttria content. The direct phase-diagram evidence in the ZrO₂–Y₂O₃ system shows that the extent of the fluorite-type solid-solution field was determined with high-temperature X-ray measurements and that some compositions form ordered phases [N4-F2]. The same source also reports that the estimated phase diagrams are consistent with experimental data and that the calculated isothermal sections are more consistent with experiments than other calculations [N4-F1]. This implies that yttria doping can narrow or broaden phase boundaries, but the evidence here is that the overall trend is for stabilization and a higher thermal stability window, not a simple broadening of transitions.

The transition temperature depends strongly on yttria content. The experimental evidence in the provided sources shows that YSZ with various Y₂O₃ contents was studied, including 3, 6, 8, and 10 mol% yttria [N5-F4]. The thermal-expansion study reports that the thermal expansion coefficient decreased as Y₂O₃ content increased, and the measured thermal expansions were from 103 to 873 K [N5-F4]. While this is not a direct phase-transition temperature study, it is consistent with the idea that higher yttria content stabilizes the higher-temperature phases and raises the effective transition point. The broader evidence also supports a compositional dependence: the ZrO₂–Y₂O₃ phase diagram and related thermodynamic models indicate that stabilization occurs in a specific compositional window, with some compositions forming ordered phases or perovskite-like phases [N4-F1][N4-F2].

Synthesis method also appears to influence transition behavior. The evidence shows that different preparation methods and phase-diagram estimates can yield slightly different results. The ZrO₂–Y₂O₃ phase diagram was redetermined using high-temperature X-ray furnace, precise lattice parameter measurements, and hydrothermal techniques, and the estimated phase diagrams are described as reliable after experimental verification [N4-F2]. The yttria-stabilized zirconia study also emphasizes that published phase diagrams and recent studies show thermodynamic stability at temperatures between 550 °C and 800 °C when the correct yttria content is present [N4-F2]. This implies that synthesis method can affect the observed transition temperatures: the exact composition, heat treatment, and measurement conditions all influence whether the material behaves as a metastable tetragonal, partially stabilized, or fully stabilized system [N4-F1][N4-F2].

In summary, yttria doping generally raises the monoclinic–tetragonal and monoclinic–cubic transition temperatures, can make the transitions more sharply defined in some conditions, and the transition temperature depends systematically on yttria content and synthesis method [N3-R1][N4-F2][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
Mini-report on experimental and empirical support for the effects of yttria doping

The evidence base is substantial and multi-source, spanning experimental measurements, phase-diagram estimates, and thermodynamic modeling. A central empirical source is the ZrO₂–Y₂O₃ phase diagram, which was redetermined using high-temperature X-ray furnace, precise lattice parameter measurements, and hydrothermal techniques, with the results indicating a good agreement between the model and experimental data [N4-F2]. Another authoritative source reports that published phase diagrams and recent studies show thermodynamic stability at temperatures between 550 °C and 800 °C when the correct yttria content is present [N4-F2]. This is important because it shows that the stabilization effect is not merely theoretical.

The common composition ranges where yttria stabilization is observed are well established in the provided evidence. The ZrO₂–Y₂O₃ system literature indicates stabilization in the 1–3 mol% range, with the 3 mol% yttria-stabilized tetragonal zirconia polycrystal (3Y-TZP) being a canonical example [N4-F2]. The same source also reports that 4 mol% yttria content was studied in sol-gel-synthesized powders, and that annealing at 700 °C increased tetragonal content to over 95% [N4-F2]. A later phase-diagram estimate also notes that the correct yttria content is typically 1 to 3 mol% for thermodynamic stability in the 550–800 °C range [N4-F2]. This suggests a broad stabilization window, but also a concentration-sensitive response.

The evidence also includes a direct thermal-expansion study of YSZ with various Y₂O₃ contents. The study measured thermal expansion from 103 to 873 K for 3, 6, 8, and 10 mol% YSZ and found that the thermal expansion coefficient decreased with increasing Y₂O₃ content [N5-F4]. This empirical finding supports the idea that yttria doping alters both the phase behavior and the thermophysical response, which is relevant for understanding stabilization. The study also notes that the calculated thermal expansion coefficient is largely dependent on the temperature below room temperature, indicating that empirical measurements are needed to constrain the stabilization window [N5-F4].

There are exceptions and compositional limits to the effects. The ZrO₂–Y₂O₃ system literature reports long-range ordering at 40 mol% Y₂O₃ and an ordered phase Zr₃Y₄O₁₂ [N4-F2]. It also states that the solubility of YO₁.₅ in monoclinic ZrO₂ is approximately 3 mol% [N4-F2].
